utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number, IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Brdjanin, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you hearing me in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hear and I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Anna Richterova, Ann Sutherland, and Denise Gustin for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Where's Ms. Gustin? I can't see her.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: She's here. She just left for two binders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I thought there was something wrong. Appearances for Mr. Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman. I'm here with Milan Trbojevic. Ms. Jevtovic is not here. It probably has to do with the storm we had yesterday and flights and things. I hope she'll be here soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ackerman. And good morning to you both. Any preliminaries? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Okay. So I will start. It has -- it is about three motions which were filed by Defence lawyers of Mr. Talic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop. I'm not interested to hear about those.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: In that case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You know that the composition of the Chamber in Talic has been changed, as of last week. And therefore, any submissions in relation to that case on behalf of either the Prosecution or the Defence ought to be addressed to a different Chamber, not to this one.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I only thought that the one motion, motion to prevent the Prosecution from introducing evidence relating to General Talic in Brdjanin case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Forget it. I mean, that will -- that will be -- I'm not interested in hearing anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: In that case, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And please proceed, because we have been discussing amongst ourselves and we will be introducing a new system in this Chamber. When you have submissions to make on a legal argument, we are not going to entertain any further oral submissions which will take time from our schedule for the hearing of witnesses. So any oral arguments which you have, which you might have, as from now onwards which are tantamount to a specific request or remedy, please henceforth be advised to formulate them in writing. But we will not entertain any further loss of time from the hearing of witnesses. The Chamber is here to hear the witnesses primarily and to deal with the rest during other hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I understand, and I do not have any preliminaries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, after what she just said, Your Honour, I don't know if I should say anything or put it all in writing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I mean, you can advise the Chamber what to expect, but just leave it at that, because it may well be that -- some kind of debate might be required.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'll limit it to one matter, Your Honour. As you know, you have and you've been given a copy of a joint memorandum that was entered into between the Prosecution and Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Regarding the Prijedor phase of the case. That memorandum by its specific terms and in its spirit contemplates that we will dramatically shorten --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- the evidence presentation in Prijedor by using transcripts of prior testimony as the basis of the direct testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Supplemented by very brief additional direct, having to do with specific Brdjanin issues. That's what Your Honour suggested; that's what we agreed. The first of those witnesses is 7.178, who's the next witness to be called. As a matter of fact, with regard to that witness, I advised the Prosecution that I would accept the transcripts without the witness even needing to be called. The Prosecution decided not to accept that offer and to go ahead and call the witness in any event. And then this morning when I got up I was greeted with a list of proposed exhibits for that witness. It appears that the Prosecution is going to put in as many as 48 documents -- have this witness talk about as many as 48 documents. It seems to me it goes way beyond the limited direct specific to the Brdjanin case. And if that's going to be the attitude of the Prosecution regarding the agreement, then I don't know why we spent any time entering into it in the first place. And it seems to be a waste and that we're just going to go forward as usual. And that's what I wanted to bring to your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But that's not a legal matter. That's a matter of administration. And what I said earlier -- what I hinted at earlier as the henceforth future policy of this Trial Chamber does not relate to matters of administration. Matters of administration need to be addressed at the beginning of the sitting as much as possible. I have a list of potential exhibits, and mine is only of 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You're looking at today's witness, Your Honour. I'm looking at --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm looking at the first one that has -- that involves transcripts. This witness there are no previous transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 7.178 is the one I'm talking about, which is the witness scheduled probably for tomorrow. And I think there are 48 -- I counted it quickly, but I think there are 48 exhibits listed there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would suggest that you thrash it out with Ms. Korner as much as you can -- or is the next witness in your hands, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. Is the next witness ...?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The next witness will be --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. He'll be testifying tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, 7.178; correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, did Your Honour want me to respond to this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please. But it could well be that these are the documents that are covered or referred to in his -- no?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, they're not, Your Honour. These documents are part of the Prijedor binders, the five binders that have been submitted as potential exhibits. A number of them -- I can't count off the top of my head, but perhaps 25 to 30 of them are dealing with dismissals and appointments. Now, we say that is relevant to Mr. Brdjanin, and this witness will not be dealing at great length with these documents and it will not take a lot of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But it's -- it's still -- I can understand Mr. Ackerman's complaints in the sense that if he's given one scenario in the beginning which is enough for him to take a decision even to the extent of not calling -- of not needing the witness to be present and then all of a sudden be informed that the witness is going probably to be referred to in the short direct to 48 documents, then the whole -- the whole picture changes --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's my understanding that Mr. Ackerman was informed last week by the senior trial attorney that this witness was going to be called by us after we had received his e-mail to say that he was happy for this witness not to be called. There was a discussion held, and he was advised that this witness was going to be called -- a few documents were going to be introduced through him from the Prijedor binders and some videos. That's my understanding of the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. In any case, let's close the debate on this matter here. May I suggest to you that knowing and fully aware that what's going to happen with Prijedor is the result of a mutual decision to cooperate between -- a mutual decision between Prosecution and Defence, I think the rest, how you administer the evidence stage in regard to this Prijedor, has to be proceeded with in the same spirit of collaboration. So in other words, please do not create situations or bring about situations which may to any extent -- because in these instances when there is good faith and cooperation, even the slightest irritation irritates more than usual. So what I would suggest is that you take these matters up in the same spirit that you have done so far and try to sort these things out in as practical --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I will have a discussion with Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And then I will discuss it with Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we call the witness in? Any further submissions Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I hesitate to ask but I was wondering what the status of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 98. Yes, a decision is on its way from Belgium, because it was drafted but it needed some more drafting, some amendments, and we still have to go through it, the three of us. It will be handed down very soon. The only thing that I can tell you before we hand down the decision is that in this we are perfectly entitled to say that the decision will not be such as to hamper or obstruct the continuation of the Prosecution proceeding with the witnesses for the time being. Okay? Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think in that connection I should report to the Trial Chamber that I -- that I worked every day since last Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So have we.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Numerous hours, 10, 12, 14 hours a day. It's my considered judgement that I have managed to work through about 20 per cent of the workload that needs to be done to be prepared for the Prijedor phase of this case. And I am absolutely prepared for the three witnesses that are scheduled for this week. No problem with any of those. Next week becomes a serious problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Next witness, please, 7. --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: He's in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In closed session. So members of the public, I'm afraid your presence in the public gallery practically comes to an end here, because we need to go into closed session with this witness for -- as a protective measure. We'll go into closed session now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: at 1.45 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 29th day of October, 2002, at 2.15 p.m.
